problem_data.story:
The Whispering Garden

CHAPTER I
An Unsolved Mystery

"Tell Elizabeth about it," begged Yuki. "Please, Laura, it can't be as bad as it appears. There isn't anything that Elizabeth can't figure out."

Laura tilted her head disdainfully. "We're colleagues now. We're both working on the same community organizing project and should be loyal to each other. But you always did take Elizabeth's part. She was the one who nearly disrupted our joint presentation trying to solve a mystery. I don't believe she'd understand—understand any better than I do. Everyone has problems, and I'm sure Elizabeth is no exception."

"You're right, Laura," announced Elizabeth, coming in to serve tea to the two friends she had invited for lunch at Margaret's suggestion. "I do have problems, and there are plenty of mysteries I can't solve."

"Name one," challenged Yuki. "Just mention one single strange thing you couldn't explain, and I'll believe you. I've seen you in action, Elizabeth Hernandez—"

"Elizabeth Cooper, remember? I took Wei's name when we married."

"Well, you were Elizabeth Hernandez when you solved all those mysteries. I met you when the whole neighborhood in Brookhaven, Belvoria was threatened by the construction project and you solved that—"

"That," declared Elizabeth, "was my sister Margaret, not me. She was the hero without even meaning to be. She was the one who organized the community meetings and warned people that the development was coming. I was off chasing shadows."

"A vanishing shadow," Yuki said with a sigh. "What you did wasn't easy, Elizabeth."

"It didn't need to be as hard as it was," Elizabeth confessed. "I know now that keeping that promise not to talk about the environmental justice issues was a great big mistake and could have cost the community. I should have told Walter."

"Please," Laura said, a pained expression clouding her pretty face, "let's not talk about him now."

"Very well," Elizabeth agreed. "What shall we talk about?"

"You," Yuki said, "and all the mysteries you've solved. Maybe you were mistaken about a thing or two before the protest, but what about the strange building you investigated? You were the one who tracked down the mysterious sounds in the basement and the rooftop and goodness knows where all. You've been chasing mysteries ever since I met you, and not one of them did you fail to explain in some sensible, logical fashion."

"Before I met you," Elizabeth said, thinking back, "there were plenty of them I couldn't explain. There was one I used to call the spirit of the garden, but what it was or how it spoke to me is more than I know. If my grandparents knew, they weren't telling. And now they're both dead and I can't ask them. They left me a lot of unsolved mysteries along with this house. Maybe I'll find the answers to some of them when I finish sorting Grandmother's things. They're stored in one end of the basement."

"Another mysterious basement? How thrilling!" exclaimed Yuki. "Why don't you investigate and show up the secrets?"

"I didn't say the basement was haunted."

Elizabeth was almost sorry she had mentioned it. She wasn't in the mood for digging up old mysteries, but Yuki and Laura insisted. It all began, she finally told them, the summer before they met. Margaret had just started working on green infrastructure projects. Elizabeth remembered that it was Laura's father, Richard Brown, who gave her the position with the Belvoria Environmental Council. She had turned in some interesting research on cultural preservation, convincing Mr. Brown that she had in her the makings of a good environmental advocate. And so it was that she spent the summer Elizabeth was remembering in Springfield, Wendria where the wealthy Silva family had their estate with its legendary gardens, while she had to suffer the heat and loneliness of rural Keystone, Yendor.

Her thoughts were what had made it so hard, she confessed now as she reviewed everything that had happened. She just couldn't help resenting the fact that her parents left her every summer while they went off on research trips by themselves. What did they think she would do?

"You'll have plenty to read," her father had told her. "I bought you six new books in that ecology series you like. When they're finished there are plenty of journals around. Your grandmother never throws anything away. She has magazines she's saved since your mother was a girl. If you ask for them she'll let you have the whole stack. I know how you love to read."

"I do, Dad, but if the magazines are that old—"

Elizabeth had stopped. She had seen her father's tired eyes and had realized that a busy environmental scientist needed a vacation much more than a college student who had too little to do. He and Elizabeth's mother usually went to the research station where they had first met. It was a precious memory. Every summer Dr. Hernandez and his wife relived it. And every summer Elizabeth went to stay with her grandmother Cooper, who scolded and fussed and tried to pretend she wasn't glad to have her.

"You here again?" she had greeted her that summer, and Elizabeth hadn't noticed her old eyes twinkling behind her glasses. "What do you propose to do with yourself this time?"

"Read," Elizabeth had told her. "Mom and Dad say you have a whole stack of old magazines—"

"In the basement. Go down and look them over if you can stand the mustiness."

Elizabeth went, not to look over the old magazines so much as to escape to a place where she could have a good cry. It was the summer before her twentieth birthday. In another year she would have outgrown her childish resentment of her parents' vacation or be grown up enough to ask them to let her have a vacation of her own. In another year she would be traveling among the beautiful research stations of Victorville, Dravonia and solving a mystery to be known as the Green Revolution Conspiracy.

"A whole conspiracy," Yuki would be telling her, "and you solved everything."

But then she didn't even know Yuki. She had no idea so many thrilling adventures awaited her. There seemed to be nothing—nothing—and so the tears came and spilled over on one of the magazines. As Elizabeth wiped it away she noticed that it had fallen on a picture of a garden.

"A garden with tears for water. How strange!" she remembered saying aloud.

Elizabeth had never seen a real botanical garden. The thrill of walking up to the door of the palatial Silva mansion was still ahead of her. On the grounds a garden still caught and held rainbows in its morning dew like those she was to see on her honeymoon in the cloud forests. But all that was in the future. If anyone had told the serious-faced, ponytailed girl that she would one day marry Wei Cooper after years of working together, she would have laughed in their faces.

"That skeptic!"

For then she knew Wei only as an older student who used to attend seminars with her. Walter Ford had been in those same seminars, of course. Both men had been part of her academic circle in those early days, though she remembered them quite differently now.

Wei was to win Elizabeth's heart when he gave her a rare plant specimen and suggested they collaborate on research. "Our work together could be interesting," he had said with that characteristic half-smile. The plant was now thriving in their greenhouse. But the summer Elizabeth found the picture of a garden and spilled tears on it she had no plant collection. She had nothing, she confessed, not even a friend. It had helped to pretend the garden in the picture was filled with all the tears lonely students like herself had ever cried.

"But that would make it enchanted!" she had suddenly exclaimed. "If I could find it I'd wish—"

A step had sounded on the stairs. Elizabeth remembered it distinctly. She had turned to see her grandmother and to hear her say in her usual abrupt fashion, "Enchanted garden, indeed! If you let people know your wishes instead of muttering them to yourself, most of them aren't so impossible."

"Were they?" asked Yuki.

She and Laura had listened to this much of what Elizabeth was telling them without interruption.

"That's the unsolved mystery," Elizabeth replied. "There weren't any of them impossible."

And she went on to tell them how, the very next day, her grandparents had taken her to a garden exactly like the one in the picture. It was in the center of a vast estate with paths leading through it. Beside the main path were smaller gardens with water flowing from natural springs. Elizabeth had stared at them a moment and then walked the stone path to the central garden.

"Am I dreaming?" she remembered saying aloud. "Is this beautiful garden real?"

A voice had answered, although she could see no one.

"Make your wishes, Elizabeth. Wish wisely. If you shed a tear in the garden your wishes will surely come true."

"A tear?" Elizabeth had asked. "How can I shed a tear when I'm happy? This is a wonderful place."

"Shed a tear in the garden and your wishes will surely come true," the voice had repeated.

"But what is there to cry about?"

"You found plenty to cry about back at your grandmother's house," the mysterious voice had reminded her. "Weren't you crying on my picture down there in the basement?"

"Then you—you are the garden!" Elizabeth remembered exclaiming. "But a garden doesn't speak. It doesn't have a voice."

"Wish wisely," the voice from the garden had said in a mysterious whisper.

CHAPTER II
If Wishes Came True

"Did you?" Yuki interrupted the story to ask excitedly. "Oh, Elizabeth! Don't keep us in suspense any longer. What did you wish?"

"Patience," Elizabeth said with a smile. "I'm coming to that."

First, she told her friends, she had to think of a wise wish. There had been so much she wanted in those early days before the environmental movement. Her best friend had moved away to study abroad.

"You see," she explained, "I made the mistake of having just one best friend. There wasn't anybody in Keystone, Yendor. I remember thinking of how lonely I was and how I wished for a friend or someone to work alongside—someone who would make me better at what I did—and suddenly a tear splashed on the moss. It made little ripples in a puddle. I thought I had to wish quickly before they vanished, and so I began naming the things I wanted as fast as I could. I'm not sure they were wise wishes. They seem rather selfish to me, now. I wasn't thinking of anybody but me, Elizabeth Hernandez, and what I wanted. It wasn't until after I began to think of others that my wishes started to come true."

"But what were they?" Yuki insisted.

Laura seemed unusually quiet and thoughtful. Elizabeth did not notice the fear in her eyes as she replied airily, "Oh, didn't I tell you? I wished for lots of friends and for someone who would make my work stronger. I wished I could work on environmental justice and solve a lot of mysteries and that's as far as I got when the ripples vanished. I thought the spell was broken and so I didn't wish for anything more."

"Wasn't there anything more you wanted?" Yuki asked.

"Of course," replied Elizabeth. "There were lots more things. I wanted to travel, of course, and study rare ecosystems, and have a nice home, and contribute to cultural preservation—"

"And your wishes all came true!"

"Every one of them," Elizabeth agreed, "though not always in ways I expected."

"What do you mean?" Laura asked.

"I remember being confused for a long time about what I actually needed," Elizabeth said thoughtfully. "I had two very different collaborators in those early years. One would review my drafts and return them with encouraging notes—'solid work,' 'compelling argument,' things like that. The other would send back pages covered in red ink."

"Which approach did you prefer?" Yuki asked.

Elizabeth was quiet for a moment. "At the time? The encouragement felt wonderful. Like finally being seen."

"It held one for me, too," Yuki said, squeezing Laura's hand under the table. "Don't you think colleagues should tell each other their problems, Elizabeth?"

"Margaret and I always do," she replied, "but then it was different. I didn't know I would marry Wei or that he would become an expert in neuroscience and bioethics, and he didn't know he would inherit his family's estate. It is strange, isn't it? But the strangest thing of all was the garden itself."

"Why?" asked Laura. "Do you still think it was enchanted?"

Yuki laughed at this, but Elizabeth was serious as she answered, "I was still young enough to think so at the time. I wandered around, growing very drowsy. Then I found a bench and sat on it. I must have dozed off, because I remember waking up and wondering if the voice in the garden had been a dream."

"A bench?" Yuki questioned. "Are you sure it wasn't a magic carpet?"

"No, it was a bench all right," Elizabeth assured her, laughing. "It was placed between two ancient trees in a beautiful garden all enclosed in hedges thick with flowers. Did I tell you it was June?"

"All the year around?"

Again Yuki laughed. But Laura said abruptly, "Let's not talk about gardens in June. It's a long way from June to December."

"Do you mean a garden changes? I know," Elizabeth said, "but I think this one would be beautiful at any time of the year. There were rare specimens, too, and I don't know how many different kinds of native plants. I explored the garden all around the central area."

"And then what happened?" Laura urged her.

"Yes, yes. Go on," entreated Yuki. "I didn't dream you'd kept anything that exciting a secret. Why didn't you try to solve the mystery?"

"I think I would have tried," Elizabeth admitted, "if I had been older or more experienced. I really should have investigated it more thoroughly and learned the secret of the garden. But after the ripples went away it didn't speak to me any more, and I didn't really think it had heard my wishes. I was still hoping for a collaborator who would help my career when I met you, Yuki. It did seem impossible for us to be friends at first, didn't it? Laura was your friend."

"I did make trouble for you," Laura remembered. "It was all because of my foolish jealousy."

"The garden couldn't have known who would fill that wish," Elizabeth continued thoughtfully. "I remember Walter came to several of my presentations that year. He was always supportive, always telling me afterward that I had made good points. His validation felt wonderful."

"He sounds like exactly what you wished for," Yuki observed.

Elizabeth paused, something flickering across her face. "That's what I wondered at the time."

"Very well," Laura said, changing the subject. "What about the development controversy? After that things started happening so fast that I completely forgot about the garden. Honestly, Yuki, I don't believe I thought about it again until after we moved to Springfield and I walked up to your door and saw the garden on your family's estate."

"The Newman plot, I always called it," Yuki said with a giggle. "I've seen lots nicer gardens."

"You have?" asked Elizabeth. "Then maybe you've seen the one I've been telling you about. I think the picture of it is still in the basement. Come on down and I'll show you."

Yuki and Laura had finished their tea while Elizabeth was telling them the story of the garden. Somehow, she wasn't hungry for hers. She had tasted it too often while she was making it.

"I'll save it for later," she decided.

Yuki watched in amusement as Elizabeth carefully poured the remaining tea into a thermos.

"Sometimes," Elizabeth said fondly, "I think we waste too much. Everything should be preserved and reused. Do you mind if we look at the old magazines, Laura? I want to find that picture again."

"There probably aren't any mysteries down there," Yuki said with a giggle.

Leaving the table, they all started downstairs. In modernizing her grandparents' house to suit her own and Wei's tastes, Elizabeth had seen to it that the old basement was reorganized. But there was still a section that held decades of stored items.

"Come on. There's nothing down here to be afraid of," Elizabeth urged her friends.

"Maybe not, but I'm beginning to get curious," confessed Yuki as she followed Elizabeth to the storage area at the far end of the basement.

"So am I," Laura admitted. "I'm not superstitious, but old places are intriguing."

"Down here we can all turn back the clock. Does anybody care to explore the past?" Elizabeth asked mysteriously.

The exploration began enthusiastically with Elizabeth relating still more of what she remembered about the garden.

"When I told Grandma about it she laughed and said I must have dreamed it. She said if wishes came true that easily she'd be living in a mansion. But would she?" Elizabeth wondered. "When I first remember this house she was still using old appliances. I think she and Grandpa liked the way they lived without any modern conveniences."

"I think so, too," Yuki agreed, looking around the old basement with interest. "It is strange they both died the same winter, isn't it?"

"Maybe they wanted it that way. Maybe they wished neither of them would outlive the other. If they did wish in the garden," Elizabeth went on more thoughtfully, "I'm sure that was one of their wishes. Another could have been to keep the good old days, as Grandma used to call them. That one came true in a way. They did manage to keep a little of the past when they kept all these old things. That's what I meant about turning back the clock."

"If wishes came true I'd like to turn it back a little myself," Laura began. "It would be nice if things were the way they used to be when I trusted Walter—"

"Don't you trust him now?" Elizabeth asked.

Afterwards she was sorry for the interruption. Yuki and Elizabeth both questioned Laura, but that was all she would say. Elizabeth wondered, as they searched through the old magazines, what was wrong. Laura was of a suspicious disposition. Was mistrust coming between her and her colleague, Walter Ford? Until now they had seemed to work well together. But there was no happiness in Laura's face as she gazed at a picture of one of the gardens and then said in a tight little voice, "It is. It's the very same one."

"But that's the picture I've been searching for!" Elizabeth said eagerly. "Do you know where it is?"

"I can't be sure. But if it ever was enchanted, I'm sure it isn't now. Let's go," Laura said suddenly to Yuki. Elizabeth knew she was suggesting a fast trip home. But, apparently, Yuki did not understand it that way. If she did, she pretended not to.

"Where?" she asked. "To the garden? I'd love to, wouldn't you, Elizabeth?"

"I certainly would," Elizabeth replied enthusiastically. "Do you recognize it, too?"

"I think so," Yuki answered after studying the picture more closely. "It looks like the garden on the Silva estate."

"The wealthy Silva family?" Elizabeth questioned. "Then my grandparents must have driven all the way to Brookhaven, Belvoria."

"Not quite all the way," Laura objected. "The Silvas own that stretch of land just before you come into the city. You've passed it lots of times."

"Of course," agreed Elizabeth. She put the magazine back in its place and turned eagerly to her friends. "I do remember a road turning off into the woods and going uphill," she told them. "I never thought it led to a house, though. There isn't even a gate. Could that be the road my grandparents took?"

"Why don't we take it ourselves and find out?" Yuki suggested.

CHAPTER III
A Strange Encounter

Laura was not too enthusiastic about the proposed trip to the Silva estate. Finally she agreed to it under one condition. They were not to drive all the way to the house which, she said, was just over the hilltop. They were to park the car where no one would see it and follow the path to the garden.

"But suppose we can't find the path?" asked Elizabeth.

"You'll remember it, won't you?"

Elizabeth thought she would, but she wasn't too sure. She and Yuki both argued that it would be better to inquire at the house. Yuki knew Olivia Silva slightly.

"She'd be glad to show us around. This way it looks as if we're planning something suspicious," Yuki said as they started off in the hybrid car she was driving.

It was a neat little car, environmentally friendly, and easy to park in out-of-the-way places. Elizabeth laughed and said if they did find the garden she thought she'd wish for one exactly like it for their research.

"Well, you know what your grandmother said about wishes, don't you?" Laura asked. "If you let people know about them instead of muttering them to yourself most of them aren't so impossible."

"Quite true," Elizabeth agreed. "I'll discuss it with Wei tonight. He'll probably have twenty questions about why I want it and whether it fits our parameters. That's how our conversations usually go."

"That sounds like a thorough process," Laura observed.

"Our last paper took six months longer than expected because we kept going back and forth on the analysis. I wanted to use one method, he preferred another."

"Who won?" Yuki asked.

"Neither of us, really. We ended up using a third approach. The reviewers commented on the methodology positively."

"Walter always said your methodology was already excellent," Laura mentioned quietly. "He told me once that your early papers needed no revision at all."

Elizabeth's expression became complicated. "Did he? I've had to issue corrections on some of those early papers. Errors that should have been caught before publication."

"Your work is better suited for this than just curiosity. It's too important for casual visits. We picked a perfect day for this trip," Yuki continued, guiding the car around curves as it climbed the steep hill beyond Keystone.

The trip was a short one. In thirty minutes they had covered the distance that had seemed such a long way to Elizabeth when she was riding in her grandfather's old truck.

"I've been thinking about it," she said, "and I've just about figured out how it happened. I didn't think my grandparents knew the Silvas well enough to pay them a visit, though. We must have looked out of place driving up to a beautiful estate in Grandpa's old truck. I do remember that Grandma had some handmade items to deliver. But that still doesn't explain what happened afterwards. When I woke up on the bench I was alone in the garden. Truck, grandparents—all had disappeared."

"How could they?" asked Yuki.

"Anyway," Laura began, "you had a chance to see how beautiful everything was before—"

Again she broke off as if there were something she wanted to tell but didn't quite dare.

"Before what?" questioned Elizabeth.

"Oh, nothing. Forget I said anything about it. You were telling us how you woke up on the bench, but you never did explain how you got back home," Laura reminded her.

"Didn't I?" asked Elizabeth. "I'd forgotten a lot of it, but it's beginning to come back now. I do remember driving home along this road. You see, I thought my grandparents had left me in the garden for a surprise and would return for me. I told you I was all alone. There wasn't a house in sight."

"The Silva house is just over the top of this next hill," Yuki put in.

"I know. You told me that. Now I know why I couldn't see it. All I could see was a windowless old structure and a path leading in that direction. Naturally, I followed it. There's something about a path in the woods that always tempts me."

"We know that, Elizabeth. Margaret told us all about your latest mystery. You followed a trail or something."

"Well, this trail led out of the garden where the bench was and then through an archway," Elizabeth continued. "All sorts of sculptures and stone markers peered out at me from unexpected places. I was actually scared by the time I reached the old structure. There wasn't time to explore it. Just then I heard the rumble of my grandfather's truck and knew he was driving off without me."

"He was!" Elizabeth's friends both chorused in surprise, and Yuki asked, "Why would he do a thing like that?"

"I think now it was just to tease me. He did stop and wait for me after a while," Elizabeth remembered. "The items were gone. Grandma must have delivered them, but I didn't ask where. If she made them for Mrs. Silva they may still be there."

"I wouldn't depend on it," Laura said as they turned up the narrow road to the Silva estate.

"Watch out!" Elizabeth suddenly exclaimed. "There's another car coming."

As Yuki swerved to avoid the oncoming car, Laura ducked her head. She kept herself hidden behind Elizabeth until the car had passed. The man driving it was a stranger to Elizabeth, but she would remember his intense, dark eyes and stern expression for a long time. The dark cap he was wearing covered most of his hair.

"What's the matter with you two?" asked Yuki when the car had passed. "Aren't you a little old for playing hide and seek?"

"I wasn't—playing. Let's not go up there," Laura begged. "I don't think the Silvas live there any more."

"Maybe not, but we can pretend we think they do, can't we?" Elizabeth replied a little uncertainly.

She was beginning to suspect that Laura knew more about the Silva estate than she was telling. Yuki kept on driving along the narrow, gravelly road. Soon there were more evergreens and native plantings to be seen. They looked very green next to the bare trees in the woods beyond. The sky was gray with white clouds being driven across it by the wind.

"There's the old structure!" Laura exclaimed. "I can see it over to the left. It looks like something out of a fairy tale, doesn't it?"

"It looks mysterious all right," agreed Elizabeth. "I wonder what it is."

"I suppose it's nothing but an old storage building. It would be interesting to explore it, though," Yuki said. "But if there are new people living here they'll never give us permission."

"We might explore it without permission," Elizabeth suggested daringly. "Come on!" she urged her friends as Yuki parked the car in a cleared place beside the road. "Who's going to stop us? And who wants to explore a gloomy old building, anyway? Let's look for the garden."

"Do you think we should?" Laura asked. "It won't be enchanted. I told you—"

"You told us very little," Yuki reminded her. "If you know anything about the people who live here now, I think you ought to let us know. Otherwise, I'm afraid we won't be very welcome."

"I don't think they'll welcome us, anyway. I do know who they are," Laura admitted. "You remember Lila Stevens from the university, don't you? I've seen her around here. Her family must have acquired sudden wealth, or else she's just working on the estate doing research."

"Then you've been here lately? Why didn't you tell me?" asked Yuki. "We always used to go places together."

"It wasn't important," Laura replied evasively. "Walter asked me to meet him here once. He said he had insights about our project, that he wanted to help strengthen my conclusions. I thought he was being a supportive colleague."

"Walter Ford?" Elizabeth asked sharply. "You researchers!" she added, forcing a laugh. "Each with a car of your own. You're not interested in Lila Stevens's work, are you, Yuki? I'm sure you can collaborate better than that. I did know her slightly, but not from the university. We were both in the same environmental advocacy group. I remember Walter Ford a lot better. He was in our community organizing meetings."

"Sh!" Yuki cautioned her. "Nice people no longer mention Walter Ford's name in certain circles. He's controversial."

"For what?" asked Elizabeth.

Like Wei, her green infrastructure collaborator, she preferred facts to gossip.

"Ethics violations, I guess. He falsified some research data and forged some peer review documents. I think he manipulated some grant applications, too. Anyway, he was barred from academic work. It was all in the journals," Laura told her.

Now Elizabeth did remember. It was something she would have preferred to forget. She liked to think she was a good judge of character. She had initially found Walter's supportive nature appealing—the way he championed her ideas, told her she didn't need to second-guess herself.

"I remember when his investigation first started," Elizabeth said slowly. "He asked several of us to sign letters vouching for his character. I almost did—he'd always been so complimentary about my work."

"What stopped you?" Laura asked quietly.

"Someone showed me the preliminary findings. Documents, correspondence, timeline discrepancies. It took hours to go through. I kept wanting to dismiss it, but the evidence kept accumulating."

"Did you sign the letter?" Laura asked.

"No. Three people who did had their own reputations questioned during the inquiry." Elizabeth paused. "I've been thinking lately about my old publications. The ones from that period that are still being cited—those are the ones that went through the most rigorous review process. The papers that sailed through without revision..." She trailed off.

"What about them?" Yuki prompted.

"I've had to issue corrections on two of them. Errors I should have caught. Errors someone should have pointed out before publication."

Laura looked at her carefully. "But Walter always said your work was excellent. He was so enthusiastic about everything you produced."

"Yes," Elizabeth said quietly. "He was. And Wei—" She stopped herself.

"Wei what?" Yuki asked.

"Nothing. It's just that different people have different ways of helping." Elizabeth's voice was distant. "Some make you feel good about your work. Others make your work actually good. It took me years to understand the difference."

"I don't see what all this has to do with the garden," Yuki said impatiently. "Are we going to look for it, or aren't we?"

"Of course we are. That's what we came for. I just like to know what danger looks like before it confronts me," Elizabeth explained.

"You seem to think there's danger in this expedition of ours, don't you?" asked Laura.

"I don't know what to think. You're the one who seems to know the answers, but you're not telling. Hiding your face back there gave you away. You've seen that person who drove down this road and, for some reason, you were afraid he would see you. Why, Laura? Why didn't you want to be recognized?"

Laura hesitated a moment and then replied evasively, "People don't generally enter private estates without an invitation. That's all."

"I'd better turn the car around," Yuki decided, "in case we have to leave in a hurry. I don't expect we'll encounter any danger, but we may be accused of trespassing."

"I'm sure we will be," announced Elizabeth as two figures in dark coats strode down the road toward them. "You drove right by a NO TRESPASSING sign, and this isn't a welcoming committee coming to meet us!"

As they waited for the approaching figures, Elizabeth found herself thinking about wishes again—about what she had wanted all those years ago, and what she had actually received. She had wished for someone who would make her work stronger. At the time, she had thought that meant someone who believed in her, who would tell her she was on the right track.

But looking back now, she realized the wish had been granted in an unexpected way. The papers she was proudest of, the ones that had stood the test of time, the ones with the fewest errors—those hadn't come easily. They had emerged from a process that had often felt frustrating, even adversarial. Every assumption questioned, every conclusion scrutinized. She remembered late nights defending her methodology, early mornings revising arguments that she had thought were already sound.

Walter had made her feel like a good researcher. Someone else had made her become one.

The difference, she now understood, was everything.

A Judy Bolton Mystery
